message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas for the staff vote

- **Chester Drawers**
- **Vanessa Veneer**
- **The Dovetail**
- **French Polish**

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

This is the **only order that works**. B has to be done by 09:30, and A can't take place before 09:00. Going to A first would put you at B at 09:40, too late. C has to be last because it won't accept anything before 11:00.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive **B**, unload |
| 09:05 | B done (25 min to spare before it opens) → drive to A |
| 09:30 | Arrive **A** (within the 09:00–10:00 window), unload |
| 09:45 | A done → drive to C |
| 10:25 | Arrive near **C**. **30-min break 10:25–10:55**, then wait |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C** |
| 11:15 | C done → drive to depot |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** |

⚠️ **There's no slack at the end.** The driver gets back at exactly 12:00, and because C can't start before 11:00, the spare time earlier in the morning doesn't help. A slow unload at C or traffic on the way back will make him late. Two ways to give yourself some breathing room:
- Phone C to ask whether they'd take it at 10:45.
- Check whether 12:00 is a hard deadline or just a target.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your delivery and should be with you in about [20] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing over furniture

1. **Condition:** no new scratches, dents or marks to the finish from the journey. Check it **with the customer present**.
2. **Completeness:** all the parts are there, such as shelves, keys, handles, feet and any fixings.
3. **Function and stability:** drawers and doors open smoothly, and the piece stands level without rocking.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Use an emailed note, with a signature taken on the driver's phone or tablet.** Emails are easier to search and file, you can attach photos of the item's condition at handover, and customers can't lose them. Keep a few paper notes in the van as a backup for customers without email or for when the signal drops.

## Proof of delivery

> Proof of delivery is the record, usually a signature, a timestamp and a photo, showing that the customer received the item in good condition.

## Evening-before text (under 160 characters)

> Hi [Name], your [Company] delivery is due tomorrow [9-11am]. We'll text when the driver's on the way. Questions? Call [number]. Thanks!

With a real example ("Sarah", "Hartley Restorations", "9-11am", "01632 960123") this comes to **147 characters**. With a long company name or customer name, check the final count.

**Avoid emoji, long dashes and curly apostrophes (’) in these texts.** Any of these switches the message to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit, so a 147-character message would be split into three. Use a plain straight apostrophe ('), as in the draft above.

For tomorrow's customers, you can give real arrival windows based on the timeline:
- **B:** around 08:50
- **A:** around 09:30
- **C:** 11:00
